subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with a 4-year history of mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) has progressive skin plaques and enlarged lymph nodes. She is started on vorinostat after failing topical therapy. Within weeks, her circulating malignant T cells show increased expression of several tumor suppressor genes.
question: Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which this drug alters gene expression?

options.text: Inhibition of histone deacetylase, increasing histone acetylation and relaxing chromatin
Inhibition of DNA methyltransferase, preventing methylation of promoter CpG islands
Inhibition of topoisomerase I, producing single-stranded DNA breaks
Increased histone deacetylation, which tightens DNA coiling and reduces transcription
Removal of methyl groups from histone lysine residues, directly activating transcription

explanation_correct: Vorinostat is a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor. Acetylation neutralizes the positive charge of lysine residues on histones, weakening their binding to negatively charged DNA, relaxing DNA coiling, and increasing transcription.

explanation_incorrect.B: DNA methyltransferase inhibitors such as azacitidine and decitabine act through hypomethylation; CpG methylation in promoters typically represses transcription, but that is not the mechanism of vorinostat.
explanation_incorrect.C: Topoisomerase I inhibitors (irinotecan, topotecan) generate single-stranded DNA breaks and are unrelated to histone acetylation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Histone deacetylation tightens chromatin and decreases transcription; this drug does the opposite by blocking the deacetylases.
explanation_incorrect.E: Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups; removal of methyl groups is not the mechanism of this drug, and histone methylation usually suppresses transcription.

educationalObjective: Histone acetylation relaxes chromatin and increases transcription, and HDAC inhibitors exploit this to reactivate silenced genes.
